name: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
title: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
answer: Vector search stores embeddings, lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables, so retrieval can respect the same joins, filters and permissions as the rest of the data. The result is one system where a similarity lookup and an ordinary SQL query can be combined in a single statement. This matters most when the rows being searched already live in the database and moving them elsewhere would be costly or risky.

sections.body: Vector search stores embeddings, lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables, so retrieval can respect the same joins, filters and permissions as the rest of the data. The result is one system where a similarity lookup and an ordinary SQL query can be combined in a single statement. This matters most when the rows being searched already live in the database and moving them elsewhere would be costly or risky.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs inside the database engine itself, on the same server or cluster that holds the relational tables. Embeddings are stored in a column type provided by the extension, and an index such as HNSW or IVFFlat is built over that column to keep nearest neighbour lookups fast. Because the index sits beside the ordinary B-tree and other indexes, the query planner can combine vector ordering with filters, joins and limits. Hardware needs are modest compared with training, though memory matters because vector indexes are typically held in RAM for speed.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical build starts by generating embeddings outside the database with an embedding model, then loading them into a vector column. Queries embed the search text the same way and ask for the rows whose vectors are closest, usually by cosine distance or inner product. The database returns the top matches, and the application can then join those rows to other tables or apply further filters. Tuning involves choosing an index type, setting parameters such as the number of lists or connections, and measuring recall against latency on real query patterns.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because vectors live in the same tables as the source records, existing access controls, row level security and audit logging can apply to retrieval as well. That is a real advantage over a separate vector store, where permissions often have to be duplicated and kept in sync. The embeddings themselves are derived data and may still carry sensitive information, so retention and deletion rules need to cover the vector column as well as the text. Provenance matters too: teams should record which model produced an embedding and when, because a model change can silently invalidate an index.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward treating vector search as one more index type rather than a separate product category. Database vendors are adding native vector types and approximate nearest neighbour indexes, and query languages are gaining distance operators and hybrid ranking that blends keyword and semantic scores. Expect more work on filtering during the index scan, on quantisation to cut memory, and on keeping embeddings fresh as source rows change. The open question is how much of the retrieval pipeline, including embedding generation, ends up inside the database.
